{"id": "29:29/q14", "question": "What does the people's demand for punishment challenge?", "turns_on": "Whether Lot had explicitly warned of punishment or his rebuke implied a judgment of vileness, liability to punishment, or prophetic authority.", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q14/p1", "position": "They challenge Lot to bring the divine punishment he warned would come.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies punishment in this world; Abū al-ʿĀliya paraphrases 'if what you say is true.' Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, and others say he warned them first; al-Thaʿlabī refers to 29:30 and says punishment was coming. Ibn ʿĀshūr says warning is an expected part of prophetic preaching although omitted earlier, and the imperative declares Lot powerless. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says another story passage attests his warning. Al-Ālūsī gives this as one reading. Al-Biqāʿī says invoking God's greatest name intensifies insolence and 'if truthful' attacks Lot's authority."}, {"id": "29:29/q14/p2", "position": "They challenge Lot's implied assertion that their conduct merits punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives this as one possible target of their reply; al-Ālūsī says the reproachful question implied that punishment was deserved."}, {"id": "29:29/q14/p3", "position": "They challenge Lot's judgment that their conduct is vile.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī offers this target; al-Ālūsī names the censured conduct's reprehensibility."}, {"id": "29:29/q14/p4", "position": "They challenge the prophethood and warning authority implied by his rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī names prophethood; al-Biqāʿī says 'if among the truthful' challenges his authority and tries to provoke him."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q15", "question": "Why did they demand punishment instead of answering Lot?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q15/p1", "position": "Their denial, obstinacy, mockery, and conviction that no punishment would come drove the taunt.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, and al-Ṭabrisī call it mockery. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī say they believed Lot false and punishment impossible; al-Qurṭubī says the wording implies settled disbelief beyond mere stubborn challenge. Rāzī says they first denied divine punishment and later threatened expulsion after continued admonition. Ibn Kathīr connects the taunt to Lot's prayer in 29:30. Al-Biqāʿī calls it ignorance, obstinacy, and provocation; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it declares Lot powerless. Study Quran compares the challenges of ʿĀd to Hūd and Thamūd to Ṣāliḥ in 46:22, 7:70, and 7:77."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q16", "question": "How can this be their only answer when other verses give an expulsion answer?", "turns_on": "Whether the two replies occurred at different times, among different speakers, in public versus private discourse, or are exclusive relative to the hoped-for response.", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q16/p1", "position": "The punishment challenge came at the first admonition; expulsion followed repeated rebukes.", "reasons": "Rāzī reads 27:56 as a later threat. Al-Irshād says the answers in 7:39 and 27:56 belong to the final dispute. Abū Ḥayyān and Abū al-Suʿūd, reported by al-Ālūsī, use early versus later stages; al-Ālūsī notes an objection that this lacks transmitted evidence and the defense that early mockery and later retaliation fit the progression."}, {"id": "29:29/q16/p2", "position": "This was their answer to Lot; expulsion was said among themselves during deliberation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this distinction with 7:82 and 27:56."}, {"id": "29:29/q16/p3", "position": "The different answers came from different groups, chiefs and others.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this reconciliation with 7:82 and 27:56."}, {"id": "29:29/q16/p4", "position": "Each exclusive formulation is relative to the response Lot hoped to receive.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says some eminent commentators appear to choose this reading."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q17", "question": "What happened after the people's challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q17/p1", "position": "Lot prayed for help and God sent angels to punish his people.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says Lot prayed against the sinful corrupters. Ibn Kathīr ties his prayer to 29:30; al-Biqāʿī says he addressed God as benefactor against a powerful people beyond his own strength. Al-Qurṭubī says the angels first visited Abraham to announce Lot's victory, referring to Hūd."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q18", "question": "What theological claim is drawn from these acts?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q18/p1", "position": "The people originated their sexual immoralities themselves, contrary to the claim that God creates human acts.", "reasons": "Jishumī directs the point against the Mujabbira doctrine."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q19", "question": "Why is Lot's call to worship God absent from this account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q19/p1", "position": "Abraham's monotheistic preaching was already known among Lot's people, so Lot stressed their distinctive offenses.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says Lot belonged to Abraham's people and compares later Abraham and Shuʿayb, who had to call to worship God. Al-Ālūsī says earlier worshippers had passed away before Abraham and Shuʿayb, referring to 29:16 and 29:36."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q20", "question": "How does this account relate to the accounts in Hūd and earlier sūras?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the difference in level of detail or simply refers to earlier discussion.", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q20/p1", "position": "Al-ʿAnkabūt details the offenses that Hūd summarizes as evil deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts 29:28–29 with 11:78; the longer account suits this sūra. He also says Lot's greater distress, the people's demand and his prayer make the messengers' arrival feel prolonged compared with 11:77, fitting the use of an, perhaps for emphasis."}, {"id": "29:29/q20/p2", "position": "This is a reprise whose detailed reading and story have been explained in earlier passages.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya refers back for a-innakum; al-Qurṭubī points to al-Aʿrāf and Hūd. Ibn al-Jazarī points back for إنكم لتأتون, Abraham's messengers, لننجينه وإنا منجوك, and سيء. Kur'an Yolu points to earlier treatments in al-Aʿrāf, Hūd, and al-Ḥijr."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q21", "question": "Why do Lot's people answer differently from Abraham's people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q21/p1", "position": "Abraham attacked idols held sacred, prompting a death threat; Lot condemned acts his people did not treat as religious duty, prompting a challenge.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares 29:24. Ibn ʿĀshūr also parallels 29:24, describing the demand for punishment as a challenge."}]}
{"id": "29:29/q22", "question": "Can two interrogatives follow one another in this construction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:29/q22/p1", "position": "Yes; a question may follow another question.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās rejects Abū ʿUbayd's objection to the double interrogative reading and says the example from this sūra used in the objection has a different construction."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q01", "question": "Who is commanded to recite, and to whom?", "turns_on": "The address is to Muhammad, but its audience and extension vary.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad is addressed, and his community also receives the command.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies People of the Book; al-Māwardī says the community; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the plural ending and 11:112."}, {"id": "29:45/q01/p2", "position": "Muhammad is told to recite for his own consolation, without a named audience.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī likens his case to earlier rejected messengers; Elmalılı reads the absence of 'to them' as a turn from provocation."}, {"id": "29:45/q01/p3", "position": "The plural forms allow an address to believers generally.", "reasons": "Asad includes 29:46 and takes revelation as what has become clear to the reader."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q02", "question": "What is the revealed Book?", "turns_on": "Whether this is the Qurʾān or an earlier book.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q02/p1", "position": "It is the Qurʾān revealed to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu argues from 'revealed to you'; al-kitāb varies by context and Ateş's own readings at 16:64, 16:89, 18:1, 13:39 and 18:49."}, {"id": "29:45/q02/p2", "position": "It is the Torah and its appendices.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports Süleyman Ateş's proposal but rejects it on the wording."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q03", "question": "What does recitation achieve and require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q03/p1", "position": "Continued, attentive Qurʾān recitation preserves, discloses and conveys its guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says universal law needs repeated transmission and exhortation softens hearts; al-Bayḍāwī and Bursevī say new readings yield new insight; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says proofs, stories and warnings deter reader and listener."}, {"id": "29:45/q03/p2", "position": "Recitation concerns whatever of divine writ becomes clear to the reader.", "reasons": "Asad links this to the verse's plural forms."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q04", "question": "What is the lexical force of tilāwa and waḥy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q04/p1", "position": "Tilāwa is reading in sequence, while waḥy is secret divine communication.", "reasons": "Bursevī allows the word revelation for speech conveyed to prophets and saints; al-Biqāʿī sees exclusive delivery as prophetic honor."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q05", "question": "What practice and merit of recitation are reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q05/p1", "position": "Recitation merits reward in differing settings and calls for humble etiquette.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports ʿAlī's scale of 100, 50, 25 and 10 deeds per letter according to posture and ablution; al-Ḥasan and jurists favor extensive recitation and long standing; Bursevī recommends ablution and facing qibla."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q06", "question": "Why are recita

tion and prayer singled out together?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q06/p1", "position": "They combine repeatable verbal remembrance and bodily action in the Prophet's mission.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the Prophet's belief was already established; al-Biqāʿī says prayer focuses attention on the Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q07", "question": "What does prayer denote here?", "turns_on": "Legal prayer, Qurʾānic recitation, and supplication are reported.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q07/p1", "position": "It is the Qurʾān recited in prayer or mosques.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar cites 17:110; al-Rāzī objects that the preceding command already names recitation."}, {"id": "29:45/q07/p2", "position": "It is the prescribed ritual prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī argues for the legal sense of a revealed term; al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī say Qurʾānic recitation is already commanded."}, {"id": "29:45/q07/p3", "position": "It is supplication or calling people to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr gives this sense; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects to departing from the apparent sense."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q08", "question": "What is required by establishing prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q08/p1", "position": "Maintain prescribed prayer fully, regularly and at its times.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites 11:114; al-Qurṭubī lists recitation, bowing, prostration, sitting and tashahhud; al-Biqāʿī says repeated practice makes sound habit."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q09", "question": "How does prayer restrain indecency and wrongdoing?", "turns_on": "Its effect may be lasting, limited to prayer time, due to recitation, or an exhortation.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q09/p1", "position": "Sincere, attentive prayer forms a lasting moral disposition, with strength varying by quality.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿĀliya names sincerity, fear and Qurʾānic remembrance; al-Rāzī invokes nearness and repeated piety; Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes renewed reminders; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes tendency from an invariable cause."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p2", "position": "It prevents wrongdoing only while the worshipper is occupied in prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says prayer interrupts sin; Ibn ʿAwn says a prayer-invalidating act leaves no prayer. Al-Rāzī argues sleep also interrupts sin, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites later repentance."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p3", "position": "Prayer may reform a continuing sinner gradually after the prayer ends.", "reasons": "The reported Anṣārī youth and thief are offered as evidence; al-Wāḥidī says later repentance shows delayed benefit."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p4", "position": "Inward remembrance and watchfulness, prayer's chief purpose, provide its restraint.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says movements alone cannot deter; Bursevī calls forgetfulness the root illness; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī makes inward awareness the intended end of speech."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p5", "position": "The Qurʾān recited during prayer is what forbids evil.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar's recitation sense and 17:110 support this; al-Jishumī also reports a reordered construction with recitation as subject."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p6", "position": "Prayer ought to restrain, as a moral instruction rather than guaranteed compulsion.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī compare sanctuary safety in 3:97; al-Qurṭubī reads the clause as an imperative in sense and cites 45:29 and 30:35."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p7", "position": "Prayer's words refute denial of God and association with Him.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī explains the opening takbīr, divine names, praise, exclusive worship, plea for guidance and testimony as repeated refutations, citing 58:2."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p8", "position": "Only some kinds or instances of prayer restrain wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this proposal but rejects it because the context concerns prayer's inherent effect."}, {"id": "29:45/q09/p9", "position": "Prayer's verbal remembrance of God alone prevents or at least reduces vice.", "reasons": "Al-Qutb links 20:14 to the thought that a praying sinner would sin still more without prayer; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects verbal remembrance alone as the intended mechanism."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q10", "question": "What does 'indecency' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q10/p1", "position": "A gravely ugly or shameless act or speech, especially fornication or adultery.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī stresses extreme ugliness; Ibn ʿĀshūr explains exceeding legal limits and cites 2:169; Kur'an Yolu includes violations of modesty and chastity."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q11", "question": "What does 'wrongdoing' mean?", "turns_on": "Reports differ between broad wrong and association with God.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q11/p1", "position": "What law, reason or virtuous custom rejects; sin and disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Wasīṭ say no revealed law or sunna recognizes it; Kur'an Yolu cites 7:157 and contrasts maʿrūf."}, {"id": "29:45/q11/p2", "position": "It means associating partners with God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās pairs this with adultery as indecency; ʿIkrima and al-Ḥasan transmit it."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q12", "question": "Why are indecency and wrongdoing paired?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q12/p1", "position": "They express distinct grounds or degrees of condemnation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says each term supplies a separate reason; al-Biqāʿī contrasts extreme ugliness with even slight wrong."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q13", "question": "What happens to prayer that does not restrain its performer?", "turns_on": "Reported wording and attribution vary.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q13/p1", "position": "It increases distance from God or divine displeasure.", "reasons": "The warning is transmitted from al-Ḥasan, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and others. Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds the mursal Prophetic chain unsound; Ibn Kathīr favors stopped reports; weak prayer leaves the sinner in prior distance rather than itself being sinful."}, {"id": "29:45/q13/p2", "position": "Prayer without restraint is no true prayer; obeying prayer means avoiding evil.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's report defines obedience to prayer; Abū al-ʿĀliya names sincerity, fear and remembrance. Ibn Kathīr prefers the stopped report; al-Durr says a Prophetic chain is weak."}, {"id": "29:45/q13/p3", "position": "Prayer without restraint becomes a burden against its performer.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda transmit this formulation."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q14", "question": "What is reported of sinners who nevertheless prayed?", "turns_on": "The Anṣārī youth and the praying thief are distinct accounts; details within each vary.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q14/p1", "position": "An Anṣārī youth prayed with the Prophet yet sinned, then repented after the Prophet foretold prayer would restrain him.", "reasons": "Some versions specify five prayers, indecency and theft; al-Ālūsī says Ibn Ḥajar could not locate the report in hadith books."}, {"id": "29:45/q14/p2", "position": "A man prayed and stole afterward; the Prophet said prayer or his recitation would restrain him.", "reasons": "Versions vary between night prayer with morning theft and day prayer with night theft. Ibn Kathīr reports al-Aʿmash's doubt and al-Bazzār's divergent chains through Abū Hurayra, Jābir and others."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q15", "question": "What reading of the statement about prayer is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q15/p1", "position": "An expanded reading says prayer enjoins right conduct and forbids indecency and wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas gives the wording; Sufyān connects prayer's commanding and forbidding with 11:87."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q16", "question": "What does prayer teach in its approach to God and return to the community?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q16/p1", "position": "Its words and postures enact nearness, humility, dependence, gratitude to the Prophet and peace to people.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī likens standing to royal service, prostration to nearness under 96:19, and salām to a returning traveler; he cites 19:72."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q17", "question": "What other reported benefit do the five prayers bring?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q17/p1", "position": "Five daily prayers wash away intervening sins like five river baths wash away dirt.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites Abū Hurayra and notes al-Tirmidhī graded the report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q18", "question": "What construction explains prayer's apparent prohibition of vice?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q18/p1", "position": "Inna gives the reason for prayer, and attributing prohibition to prayer depicts moral admonition.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares inna with causal faʾ and denies forceful compulsion; al-Kashshāf says the generic claim need not hold of every worshipper."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q19", "question": "How is prayer's acceptance recognized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q19/p1", "position": "Its acceptance is proportional to how much it restrains indecency and wrong.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh's report is transmitted by al-Ṭabrisī, al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q20", "question": "What recitational pronunciation rule applies to the cited words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q20/p1", "position": "A heavy lām accompanies open alif from yāʾ, while imāla requires light lām; Warsh's light rāʾ does not lighten Allah after fatḥa or ḍamma.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī gives the articulation rule and Warsh's treatment."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q21", "question": "What does the verse teach about divine grace and human responsibility?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q21/p1", "position": "Prayer is divine grace aiding restraint; failure to respond belongs to the worshipper.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī calls the grace obligatory; al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes God's enabling from personal failure."}]}

scribed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q22/p1", "position": "Prayer has bodily, self, heart, secret, spirit, hidden and essential levels, each restraining a corresponding fault.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī pairs these with grades of knowledge and prayer; the seventh is annihilation and returns in subsistence. Outward prayer ends at death, real prayer at annihilation; he cites 15:99."}, {"id": "29:45/q22/p2", "position": "The highest remembrance is annihilation of selfhood, in which divine remembrance surpasses human remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī identifies remembrance of the Essence in annihilation; Study Quran joins divine and human senses beyond time and place."}, {"id": "29:45/q22/p3", "position": "Accepted inward prayer averts self-admiration, demands for reward and worldly gain.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ name these faults; Bursevī recounts the dream of a man who failed to value prayer with Ḥabīb al-ʿAjamī."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q23", "question": "What does remembrance mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q23/p1", "position": "It can name the ritual prayer itself.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān states this usage; several exegetes cite 62:9."}, {"id": "29:45/q23/p2", "position": "Primarily inward recollection or presence, with speech named remembrance through its inward content.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib distinguishes retention from bringing knowledge to mind, and remembrance after forgetting from sustained awareness; Ibn ʿAṭiyya requires knowledge and attention."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q24", "question": "What is meant by 'God's remembrance is greater'?", "turns_on": "God may be the one remembering or the remembered; the comparison varies.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q24/p1", "position": "God's remembrance of people exceeds their remembrance of Him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and many others cite 2:152; al-Ṭabarī prefers it. Sources explain God's remembrance as mercy, guidance, reward, praise or uncaused grace, contrasting it with finite human need."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p2", "position": "A person's remembrance of God exceeds other deeds or everything.", "reasons": "Qatāda cites 20:14; Muʿādh and Abū al-Dardāʾ rank it over fighting and wealth; reports commend a moist tongue at death and angel-attended gatherings. Umm al-Dardāʾ includes fasting and avoiding evil."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p3", "position": "Remembering commands, prohibitions or threats at temptation restrains more than prayer alone.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and ʿUmar prefer abstention to tongue-only remembrance; Ibn ʿAbbās sometimes gives this sense but elsewhere rejects it for God's remembrance."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p4", "position": "Prayer itself, as remembrance, surpasses other acts of obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī and others cite 62:9; remembrance is prayer's source of superior merit."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p5", "position": "Remembrance within prayer is greater than the wrongdoing it prevents.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAwn contrasts the positive act with the evil prevented; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers inward remembrance as prayer's greater benefit."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p6", "position": "God's remembrance of a worshipper during prayer surpasses prayer itself.", "reasons": "Abū Mālik says so; al-Ālūsī makes God the grammatical agent. Al-Māwardī transmits a variant with the servant remembering God."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p7", "position": "God's remembrance cannot coexist with sin or its punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and ʿAṭāʾ give this inward sense; al-Māwardī mentions punishment for indecency."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p8", "position": "God's remembrance exceeds human understanding.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim says it transcends intellect and indication; al-Māwardī and al-Nasafī repeat the sense."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p9", "position": "Remembrance in prayer exceeds other pillars or remembrance outside prayer.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī report these comparisons."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p10", "position": "God's remembrance surpasses recollection of ancestors or idols.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī contrasts remembrance of ancestors; Study Quran reports the contrast with idolaters' gods."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p11", "position": "God's remembrance is supreme without a specified comparison.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim describes God's invocation as supreme; al-Rāzī sees unqualified greatness as akin to Allāhu akbar."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p12", "position": "God's prohibition of vice exceeds mere refraining from vice.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj reports this explanation."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p13", "position": "Remembrance is faith in God's existence and oneness, the root of the other acts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr relates this to the sūra's condemnation of shirk from 29:42 and cites 90:13–17."}, {"id": "29:45/q24/p14", "position": "Qurʾān recitation as remembrance is greater than prayer and more apt to restrain evil.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī allows this third reading of the phrase."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q25", "question": "How does the remembrance phrase work grammatically?", "turns_on": "The genitive and comparative form support different readings.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q25/p1", "position": "Akbar is absolute or means 'great', without a comparative complement.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says kabīr; al-Zamakhsharī makes it unrestricted superiority; Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī give noncomparative readings, the latter citing 62:11."}, {"id": "29:45/q25/p2", "position": "The genitive makes God the object of human remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī contrasts this with the agentive reading; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī applies it to alternatives about human remembrance."}, {"id": "29:45/q25/p3", "position": "The genitive makes God the one remembering, with the servant understood as object.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī states the agentive reading and al-Ālūsī notes the omitted object."}, {"id": "29:45/q25/p4", "position": "Akbar takes an omitted comparator, such as 'than everything'.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān and al-Ālūsī supply the ellipsis."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q26", "question": "How does the remembrance clause connect with its context?", "turns_on": "It may develop prayer's benefit or stand with the recitation command.", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q26/p1", "position": "It develops prayer's benefit and explains its superiority or restraint.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī name remembrance as prayer's reason; Ibn ʿĀshūr coordinates it with the prayer clause."}, {"id": "29:45/q26/p2", "position": "It is independent of prayer's preceding statement or links back to recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī explicitly separates the second view; Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to the recitation command."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q27", "question": "How does al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī assess the listed remembrance interpretations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q27/p1", "position": "Some alternative readings are arbitrary or insufficiently grounded.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī leaves the enumerated alternatives unexamined while observing the arbitrary character of some."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q28", "question": "What reports illustrate God's reciprocal remembrance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q28/p1", "position": "God remembers individuals and gatherings that remember Him.", "reasons": "Al-Thāʿlabī reports the sacred saying of reciprocity and angels surrounding gatherings; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Bursevī cite private and public remembrance."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q29", "question": "What is prayer's chief intended benefit?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q29/p1", "position": "It establishes inward awareness of God, a greater good than moral restraint alone.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls remembrance its greatest intended element; Elmalılı cites 20:14 and 2:152; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls inward awareness the highest human work."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q30", "question": "What does the closing statement about God's knowledge convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q30/p1", "position": "God knows prayer and all good and evil deeds, rewarding or requiting them; the clause warns and exhorts watchfulness.", "reasons": "Muqātil restricts the immediate scope to prayer; al-Jishumī calls it a grave threat; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it sums up the commands."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q31", "question": "What does 'what you do' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q31/p1", "position": "It means deeds or sustained work.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses ṣanʿ as deed; al-Biqāʿī hears repeated work and training in the wording."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q32", "question": "How does the verse connect with its sūra and surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q32/p1", "position": "After earlier peoples and shirk, it turns to revelation and prayer to strengthen Muhammad and the believers.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī sees consolation; Ibn ʿĀshūr sees strengthened preaching; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls revelation a deterrent after shirk's fate."}, {"id": "29:45/q32/p2", "position": "It begins an argument for the Qurʾān's miraculousness continuing through 29:46–51.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes limiting such arguments to sūra openings and cites the testing of believers and defense of revelation."}]}
{"id": "29:45/q33", "question": "What further watchfulness does the verse require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:45/q33/p1", "position": "Recitation, prayer, remembrance and God's knowledge call for lasting obedience and moral care.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī urges persistence; Kur'an Yolu warns those who violate others' rights; Bursevī says consciousness of divine knowledge should empty the heart of distractions."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q01", "question": "Why is God's name placed before the verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q01/p1", "position": "The initial divine name emphasizes that God originates creation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fronting of the divine name before the verbal predicate serves emphasis alone."}]}

 "question": "What does يَبْدَؤُا۟ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q02/p1", "position": "It means beginning an action.", "reasons": "Jishumī contrasts badʾ with ending and also with returning."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q03", "question": "How is يَبْدَؤُا۟ read?", "turns_on": "Whether the prefix has ḍamma and the dāl kasra or the dāl has the usual open vowel.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q03/p1", "position": "The usual reading opens the latter vowel.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says most readers open the dāl in contrast to the reported kasra."}, {"id": "30:11/q03/p2", "position": "The variant yubdiʾu has ḍamma on the yāʾ and kasra on the dāl.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes it to Ṭalḥah and Ibn Masʿūd; Abū Ḥayyān names Ibn ʿAbd Allāh and Ṭalḥah; Ālūsī names ʿAbd Allāh and Ṭalḥah."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q04", "question": "What is the creation God begins?", "turns_on": "Whether al-khalq names all created beings, human creation, or the historical change in the two empires' fortunes.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q04/p1", "position": "Created beings generally, brought into existence by God alone.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says creation comes from nothing by God's power, without partner or helper; Kuran Yolu reports the same from Ṭabarī and adds no prior material. Nasafī says created beings come into existence. Biqāʿī says God continually begins whatever creation He wills, as people observe. Ibn ʿĀshūr says even the polytheists must concede that God alone originated creation, citing 13:16. The Study Quran gives this as an alternative to a specifically human reading and cites 10:4, 10:34, 27:64, and 30:27. Ibn al-Jawzī says al-khalq means created beings; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the return pronoun refers to them."}, {"id": "30:11/q04/p2", "position": "Human beings in their first worldly life.", "reasons": "Muqātil, reported also by Wāḥidī, says God first created people. Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī likewise identify people. Bursevī specifies the human's creation from a drop of fluid. The Study Quran's human reading specifies first composing them from dust and cites 10:4, 10:34, 27:64, and 30:27."}, {"id": "30:11/q04/p3", "position": "The beginning is the Persians' victory over the Romans.", "reasons": "Qāshānī reads the first creation in the setting of the two empires' fortunes."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q05", "question": "What does God's repeating or restoring creation mean?", "turns_on": "Whether repetition denotes resurrection, creation after annihilation, observable renewal, both renewal and resurrection, or the historical reversal of power.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q05/p1", "position": "God revives human beings after death for resurrection.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Wāḥidī say they return alive as they were. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Nasafī, Bursevī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Asad explain the return as resurrection; Bursevī distinguishes worldly and afterlife creation. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī also call the restoration resurrection. The Study Quran describes a human body first composed from dust and then resurrected, citing 10:4, 10:34, 27:64, and 30:27. Rāzī and Iṣlāḥī say initial creation demonstrates this human restoration."}, {"id": "30:11/q05/p2", "position": "God restores creation after it perishes or is annihilated.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says God annihilates creation and makes it anew, complete as at first. Jishumī says God alone can restore after annihilation. Biqāʿī says creation perishes before God restores it; Kuran Yolu reports Ṭabarī's destruction and recreation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī summarizes the verse as God originating and repeating creation."}, {"id": "30:11/q05/p3", "position": "God continually renews creation in nature.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu offers nature's ongoing renewal as one possible sense of repeated creation."}, {"id": "30:11/q05/p4", "position": "The phrase embraces both nature's continual renewal and resurrection after Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu explicitly permits both senses together, as well as each separately."}, {"id": "30:11/q05/p5", "position": "God reverses the imperial outcome by making the Romans prevail over the Persians.", "reasons": "Qāshānī pairs this reversal with the earlier Persian victory."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q06", "question": "What does restoration mean as a term?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q06/p1", "position": "It is doing something a second time, also called return or second creation.", "reasons": "Jishumī says repetition is a second doing; restoration, return, and second creation are equivalent. He says return is literal for bodies and enduring accidents but figurative for speech, and does not apply literally to sounds."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q07", "question": "What does the singular pronoun in يُعِيدُهُۥ refer to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q07/p1", "position": "It refers back to al-khalq in its singular grammatical form.", "reasons": "Baghawī notes that the verse says He restores it rather than explicitly He restores them. Ibn al-Jawzī says al-khalq means created beings, though the singular object follows the word's form. Wāḥidī likewise contrasts the singular form here with the plural sense followed by the last verb."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q08", "question": "Must creation perish before it can be restored?", "turns_on": "Whether restoration requires the body's prior annihilation or can consist in regathering and reviving bodies that never perish.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q08/p1", "position": "Yes; restoration follows prior annihilation or perishing.", "reasons": "Jishumī explicitly argues from the word restores that annihilation must precede it. Ṭabarī describes annihilation before a new creation, while Biqāʿī and the account of Ṭabarī in Kuran Yolu also place perishing or destruction before restoration."}, {"id": "30:11/q08/p2", "position": "No; bodies need not perish, since God can regather and revive them.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports al-Jāḥiẓ's view that bodies do not perish and restoration consists in gathering and reviving them."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q09", "question": "How are bodies said to be annihilated?", "turns_on": "Whether annihilation occurs through a created opposite, direct annihilation of bodies, a nonenduring state, or a divine command alone.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q09/p1", "position": "God creates an opposite called annihilation, while bodies and their accidents remain.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this as the view of Abū ʿAlī, Abū Hāshim, and their followers."}, {"id": "30:11/q09/p2", "position": "The bodies themselves are annihilated.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this view to Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Khayyāṭ."}, {"id": "30:11/q09/p3", "position": "God creates a nonenduring state in bodies, then no subsequent state, so they cease to exist.", "reasons": "Jishumī introduces this as a further reported view."}, {"id": "30:11/q09/p4", "position": "God merely commands the bodies to perish and they perish.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls this claim a weak argument."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q10", "question": "What conditions make a thing restorable?", "turns_on": "Whether divine power must be exclusive and whether non-generation is absolute or restricted to a nonpersistent cause.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q10/p1", "position": "It can persist, is not generated, and lies within the Creator's power.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports these three conditions from the Qāḍī."}, {"id": "30:11/q10/p2", "position": "It lies within God's exclusive power, can persist, and belongs to a kind only God can restore.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports these three conditions from Abū ʿAlī."}, {"id": "30:11/q10/p3", "position": "It lies within God's power, can persist, and is not generated from a cause that does not persist.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this as another formulation, distinguishing it from the Qāḍī's unrestricted condition that the thing not be generated."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q11", "question": "How does the verse argue that God can restore creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q11/p1", "position": "God's power to originate creation establishes His power to repeat it.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the first act was by power and will, so the resurrection claim has proof. Ibn Kathīr likewise infers capacity to restore from capacity to originate. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls repetition an a fortiori inference from what polytheists already concede; Biqāʿī calls ability to repeat one's own creation self-evident. Iṣlāḥī says repeating a task is easier and answers deniers who deem resurrection far-fetched. Kuran Yolu reports Ṭabarī's argument from God's unique power without partners or prior material. Asad links new creation to 10:4 and 30:27; the Study Quran cites 10:4, 10:34, 27:64, and 30:27. Kuran Yolu also invites reflection on the wisdom of creating and recreating."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q12", "question": "Whose restoration does reason or revelation require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q12/p1", "position": "Reason requires restoration for those owed reward or unpaid compensation; revelation promises restoration of every living being.", "reasons": "Jishumī says punishment is God's right and could be omitted, while revelation includes accountable and unaccountable living beings in the promise of restoration."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q13", "question": "What does the second ثُمَّ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q13/p1", "position": "It marks a rise in rank, not simply later time.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says return to God is greater than recreation because it is the ultimate purpose of creation and resurrection."}]}

{"id": "30:11/q16", "question": "How is تُرْجَعُونَ read?", "turns_on": "The verb's person and voice: direct address or third-person narration, and passive return or active voluntary return.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q16/p1", "position": "Second-person plural passive, turjaʿūn: you are returned.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and ʿAyyāsh from Abū ʿAmr; Fārisī gives the first six and also cites Ibn ʿAbbās's report from Abū ʿAmr. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr call this the majority or general reading. Jishumī says most retain the ḍamma, unlike Yaʿqūb's open vowel. Qirāʾāt ER contrasts its passive compulsion with active agency. Wāḥidī, Zamakhsharī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and others also report the tāʾ form."}, {"id": "30:11/q16/p2", "position": "Third-person plural passive, yurjaʿūn: they are returned.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Baghawī, and Ibn al-Jawzī name Abū ʿAmr and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim. Wāḥidī, Bursevī, and Fārisī say it follows the plural sense of al-khalq and surrounding third-person narration. Abū Ḥayyān calls its readers the two fathers. Qirāʾāt ER says third person makes the return a universal cosmic principle."}, {"id": "30:11/q16/p3", "position": "Third-person plural active, yarjiʿūn: they return voluntarily.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER says the active form gives subjects agency instead of passive compulsion."}, {"id": "30:11/q16/p4", "position": "Second-person plural active, tarjiʿūn: you return voluntarily.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER says this keeps direct address while assigning human agency. Jishumī says Yaʿqūb opens the vowel throughout the Qurʾān, unlike the readers' usual ḍamma."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q17", "question": "Why change from narration to direct address at the return?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q17/p1", "position": "Direct address makes the return explicit and presses its warning on the hearers.", "reasons": "Fārisī and Wāḥidī compare the move to direct address in the Fātiḥah, citing 1:1 and 1:4 or 1:2 and 1:5. {"id": "30:11/q18", "question": "How can the final verb be plural after singular يُعِيدُهُۥ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q18/p1", "position": "The object pronoun follows the singular form al-khalq, while a third-person plural return follows its collective meaning.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī states this contrast explicitly in two notes. Fārisī says the yāʾ reading follows the plural sense of creation. Ibn al-Jawzī identifies al-khalq as created beings despite the singular object pronoun. Baghawī notes the singular reference. Bursevī says the variant third person follows al-khalq's collective sense; Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes the plural return pronoun as referring to created beings."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q19", "question": "How does this verse connect with its neighboring verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q19/p1", "position": "It supplies proof of resurrection after the deniers' fate and leads to the account of what follows their return.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the earlier mention of Hell implies resurrection, which God then proves, and 30:12 describes what happens upon return. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 30:10 recalls deniers' worldly end and the succession of nations to prepare the case for resurrection and judgment. Biqāʿī says the explicit conclusion recaps the preceding proof and affects the soul. The Study Quran describes the movement from disbelievers' failure to reflect toward the differing ends of believers and disbelievers."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q20", "question": "How does this verse express the sura's central theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q20/p1", "position": "It states God's creation, life from death, and the power and promise of resurrection.", "reasons": "Asad identifies this theme across 30:11, 30:16, 30:19, and 30:27."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q21", "question": "What distinction does final judgment make among claimants to faith?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q21/p1", "position": "God separates sincere believers from hypocrites who claim faith but avoid hardship.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says justice requires this sifting of sincere followers from mere claimants."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q22", "question": "What warnings about religious error accompany this verse?", "turns_on": "The two reports condemn different forms of religious error: kalām and denial of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q22/p1", "position": "Engaging in kalām leads to heresy, and its originator bears the burden of the innovation and its imitators until resurrection.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports al-Shāfiʿī's warning and says imitators' own burdens are not diminished."}, {"id": "30:11/q22/p2", "position": "Those who deny the Qurʾān and reduce prophetic revelation to law are cursed.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports this denunciation and repeated curses from al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyyah."}]}
{"id": "30:11/q23", "question": "Can a pronoun of separation precede an imperfect verb in a parallel expression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "30:11/q23/p1", "position": "Yes; it may precede an imperfect verb such as yubdiʾu in a related expression.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān reports al-Jurjānī applying this to huwa yubdiʾu wa-yuʿīd at 85:13, and Abū al-Baqāʾ applying it to a second example at 85:15."}]}
{"id": "31:10/q01", "question": "What does the creation of the heavens entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "31:10/q01/p1", "position": "God originated the seven heavens.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies seven; Ṭabrisī says God brought them into being; Bursevī adds the Throne and Footstool."}, {"id": "31:10/q01/p2", "position": "The heavens exist by God's power and choice, not by necessity or nature.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says this holds whether they are spherical or flat; their place in limitless space depends on divine choice."}]}
